summary: A caliphate centered in Iraq whose initial political empire later fragmented while Abbasid caliphs retained varying degrees of religious and regional authority.
currency: Gold dinars and silver dirhams; issues varied across periods and mints.
economy: Baghdad and Samarra became important commercial and cultural centers connecting regional economies.
military: Al-Mutasim established Samarra to accommodate an army including Turkish slave soldiers; later dynasties exercised much of the caliphate’s effective military authority.
contributions: Patronage of scholarship, urban architecture and ceramic techniques had a lasting influence across the Islamic world.
origin: The Abbasid dynasty replaced the Umayyads in 750 and shifted the political center from Syria to Iraq.
decline: Provincial autonomy and military dynasties eroded central power; Mongol forces sacked Baghdad in 1258.
periodNote: 1258 ends the Baghdad caliphate. Later Abbasid caliphs in Mamluk Cairo held primarily nominal authority; caliphal claims do not equal continuous territorial control.
